cards.title: AI-generated posters don’t have to be horrible

depth.text: A writer broke ChatGPT out of generic event poster designs by asking for specific historic art styles.

To avoid the default template used for village fayre flyers, the author asked ChatGPT to generate posters using aesthetics like Bauhaus, Memphis Design, and punk fanzines. Asking for specific aesthetics broke the model out of its usual repetition, leading to a catalogue of one hundred poster styles.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say AI generators produce cheaper and better flyers for local events than budget freelancers, while others say the results still suffer from obvious AI uniformity, clichés, and broken visual hierarchy.
comments: A lot of people in the comments say that the supposedly better examples in the article are still “horrible” because they can tell they’re AI and point to things that the AI did “wrong” and a human artist would do better. That may be true if you’re working with a top of the line artist, but in my experience the average freelance designer online is significantly worse than AI. I’ve worked with…

I find it kinda funny that even "smartest", most capable models often have a very hard time going beyond surface-level, top-of-mind associations, when faced with creative tasks. Of course , a "Japanese Minimal Poster" has a sakura and a stylized flag of Japan, duh A human designer would probably think that "Japan -> sakura" and "Japan -> Japanese flag" are way too obvious, too banal, too…

It’s not complicated - the default style signals low effort. Why should I get excited about the village fete if the organizers put in the barest minimum of effort? But there’s another reason it drives people crazy - it’s low effort trying to present as high effort. If the sign was simple Comic Sans then it would at least be charmingly honest.

cards.title: I built non-autoregressive decision models with RL a year ago

depth.text: A developer open-sourced Laya, a fast decision model, after a venture-backed lab branded the concept a breakthrough.

Laya evaluates structured queries using bidirectional encoders in 32.8 milliseconds, outputting calibrated probabilities instead of generating text to avoid hallucinations. Released under an Apache 2.0 license with three checkpoints across more than 100 languages, it avoids generative streaming delays. However, performance degrades on choice questions with more than 20 options, and base checkpoints require fine-tuning for strong accuracy.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say packaging, easy hosted APIs, and zero-shot convenience matter far more than academic research, while others argue both projects are just standard BERT-style classifiers dressed up in venture capital marketing.
comments: It’s a tale as old as time — people don’t understand that marketing and branding are just as important, if not more so, than the product. Jev is exceptionally-well branded. Anyone can look at the webpage and understand it, and the implications, instantly. OPs “marketing” is a single post on Reddit titled “ Predicting sales conversion probability from conversations using pure Reinforcement…

I think the main gripe that people had with Jev and Typesafe was the language used when they launched. To me personally it seemed like a parody/con/shady at first. "Breakthrough", "our research went in another direction" , "Two years in stealth", "System One thinking model", "Jev can't hallucinate", "RLCD","We are doing very cool stuff, but we will have to hire you to tell you", - these…

I played around with Jev last night and did it for classification tasks that I used Gemini 2.5 flash lite with. It’s a bit faster and bit cheaper, but this is compared to LLM. The consistency was nice to see, BUT, as someone who trained NLP models prior to LLMs, it’s just BERT with more data. I can see why people would want ready made one shot classifier, and I can see the value of sending…

I can understand why the author feels bitter but it still feels juvenile to me. Certainly both Jev and Laya are based on the research of countless prior papers and academics. Diogo decided to build a product out of the concept. The author didn't. Publishing research papers and model weights is probably part of the problem--it feels academic. If you look at the author's profile they focus on…

cards.title: ChatGPT now knows what you do on other websites via ad collector

depth.text: OpenAI built an ad tracker that connects what you do on ordinary websites to your ChatGPT account.

OpenAI uses a cross-site cookie to link what you do on partner websites back to your ChatGPT account. When advertiser pages load the company's tracking code, it sends back browsing activity alongside scraped form fields. Because OpenAI classifies the tracker as an analytics cookie, it still tracks users who refused marketing consent.

comments: I am once again happy that the EU is fighting practices like these via legislation. Some outcomes can be annoying, but the net result is still positive, for the consumers and their data privacy at least.

To me, this quote just about sums it up: > The mechanism is standard adtech. What has no precedent is running it on an AI chat product. As someone who has been well aware of this mechanism for quite some time, I still feel icky anytime I re-read the details of it. What a time to be alive.

I know people use chat bots differently and I get that companies see value in personalization, but to me it is extremely valuable that I can start a chat without context. When researching a topic a chatbot can be quite sensitive to certain wording and those can end up steering definitions. Two context free chats on the same topic can go in very different ways depending on how you word things, but…
https://www.pangram.com/history/c3ad864f-2a50-4785-a0ef-71f2... why not use your own words? If you are gonna ai generate this blog, just post the prompts instead.

cards.title: Qwen Image 2.1

depth.text: Qwen released Qwen Image 2.1, a compact 7B image model that adds native transparency but drops Apache licensing.

Qwen Image 2.1 drops from 20B down to 7B parameters, generating a 1MP image in roughly five seconds on an RTX4090. The model adds native transparency and sharp text rendering, but it explicitly forbids commercial usage without a separate license.

cards.camps: Two camps: one praises its fast local generation and sharp text rendering, while another is let down by the restrictive non-commercial license and prompt-following issues.
comments: So thoughts Positives • It's a heck of a lot smaller than Qwen-Image 1 (20b parameters) at only 7b, making it one of the smaller open-weight models available (Z-Image Turbo is one of the few that is smaller at 6b) when compared to Ideogram, Krea2, Flux2, etc. • It supports native transparency (Qwen's team, as far as I know, is the only one attempting to tackle this). Even though it's relatively…

A lot of the previous Qwen models seem to have used Apache licenses, among others: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qwen#List_of_models Unfortunately, it looks like this model is using a much more restrictive license: https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image-2.1/blob/main/LICENSE

I run a prompt-to-ui design site that uses image models for the design process[1]. The text rendering especially makes this model deeply interesting to me, despite the license. Here are some tests using my harness comparing the outputs of gpt-image-2 and qwen 2.1: https://html.non.io/qwen-comparison/ The text rendering definitely is much, much better than anything else on the…

The capabilities of local LLM text-to-image is honestly pretty damn impressive. IMO, I think local image generation is currently ahead of local code generation. I can get an image in seconds locally with the quality being way higher than what I'd expect from a local model. However with coding it's much slower and much less impressive. I'm sure there's a reason for this and I'm not an AI expert so…

The minute you start looking at other non-frontier models, you understand why Dario, Altman, and Musk are coming together to say we need regulation. None are as good yet, but what everyone said is coming true - models are not moats. And these folks need an exit (even Msuk whose shares are still locked)

cards.title: Two parallel neural ectoderm progenitors contribute to the developing brain

depth.text: Researchers showed the brain develops from two separate progenitor cell lineages instead of just one.

Mouse embryo tracing showed that two parallel progenitors emerge simultaneously to form different brain regions. The authors postulate the brain is a composite organ, using the discovery to grow hindbrain motor neurons in vitro that were previously difficult to generate.

cards.camps: Two camps: some argue calling the brain a composite organ is misleading press release spin, while others emphasize the practical breakthrough of finally being able to culture hindbrain cells in vitro.
comments: The really exciting thing in this article is that this research led them to a new technique for growing brain stem cells in vitro, which has been very difficult until now. If that isn't being oversold, it's big news. That's going to make future research into diseases like ALS a lot easier.

The actual research says something far less clickworthy. Are Stanford's PR dribbles now created by LLMs ? "Two parallel neural ectoderm progenitors contribute to the developing brain Abstract When and how different brain regions diversify from one another remains unresolved. Does a common neural ectoderm progenitor generate the entire brain? Or do multiple neural ectoderm progenitors exist, each…

cards.title: AX – Google’s Open Agentic Orchestrator

depth.text: Google engineers launched AX, an open-source tool designed to sandbox, run, and instantly freeze fleets of AI agents.

AX divides agent workloads into tasks, workspaces, gateways, and models to manage untrusted code, network rules, and credentials declaratively. It runs on Agent Substrate, packing workloads together and pausing idle agents in under a second so users only pay for active compute.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters argue that agents do not need a whole new orchestrator when standard API calls or basic Kubernetes already work, while others point out that despite promises of simple setup, AX still requires a heavy Kubernetes stack to run.
comments: So on one hand the page says > We want to make dealing with agentic infrastructure easier so you can focus on your work. cards.title: Pirate Face Rescues LLM Models from Deletion

depth.text: Pirate Face mirrors Hugging Face models as torrents so AI weights survive if the host deletes them

Each model is packaged as a torrent with a built-in web-seed that pulls directly from Hugging Face until it goes down, falling back to a peer-to-peer swarm. Every download is checked against official SHA-256 checksums to confirm the files match the original weights.

cards.camps: Two camps: some praise torrents as the ideal way to eliminate Hugging Face as a single point of failure, while critics argue the service has technical flaws and responds to exaggerated fears of model takedowns.
comments: Speaking to the "uncensored model" angle: there's little reason to distribute abliterated weights anyway. Instead of orthogonalising the weights that write back to the residual stream, you can just orthogonalise the activations themselves. It's equivalent. Orthogonalising activations at runtime is computationally cheap. Just distribute the refusal vectors (few thousand floats per layer), then run…
Torrents should really be the preferred method for distributing AI model weights. Why rely on a single point of failure like Hugging Face? BitTorrent was made for exactly this.

Steam & Blizzard (probably others) used to delivery games through torrent protocol in the past, before CDNs became cheaper. When StarCraft 2 was lauched, the installer (before Battle.net installer crapware) had a complete graphical visualization of seeders & leechers. Reference: https://warcraft.wiki.gg/wiki/Blizzard_Downloader

cards.title: Samsung is expected to more than double output of its HBM4 and HBM4E DRAM

depth.text: Samsung is gearing up to more than double output of its next-gen AI memory chips next year.

Samsung plans to expand total HBM capacity to about 250,000 wafers a month, shifting sixth- and seventh-generation chips to roughly 80% of its shipment mix. Stacking 12 layers or more requires grinding wafers paper-thin, so the company is increasing outsourced cleaning for protective glass carriers 2.5-fold to support the ramp.
data: Projected monthly HBM wafer scale next year
Projected HBM4 family share of shipment mix

cards.camps: Two camps: some worry shifting factory capacity to high-margin AI memory will make consumer RAM prices worse, while others hope expanding chip supply might finally cool down GPU prices.
comments: The article features a truck that the chips get loaded onto. This quote from Tanenbaum immediately jumped into mind: "Never underestimate the bandwidth of a station wagon full of tapes hurtling down the highway."

I’ve often wondered about die thinning. I mean just looking at sd cards and micro sd etc, it was clear that there had to be a thinning step (or many steps) and it seemed amazing to me that such a complex step could be economically viable. And yet it clearly is. All a matter of being able to operate at scale I guess. It’s not a step I’ve seen discussed very much, so it was kind of neat to see it…

cards.title: Attention is all you have

depth.text: Alice Girard Guittard argued that algorithmic feeds hijack your attention and urged a return to intentional browsing

The essay warns that modern platforms replace deliberate focus with doomscrolling, AI slop, and ad-driven recommendations, shaping what people think about via the Tetris effect. Guittard argues that a slower internet built around bookmarks, personal blogs, and RSS feeds is still intact if readers commit to seeking it out.

cards.camps: Two camps: some agree that algorithmic feeds ruin attention and advocate switching back to books and RSS, while others argue early portals like MSN and Yahoo! were always full of clickbait and algorithms just give people what they want.

depth.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced a bill to ban private equity and insurance companies from owning medical practices.

The bill would ban for-profit corporations from owning practices and prohibit management services organizations from controlling operations. It pairs mandatory divestment with enforcement paths through the FTC, state attorneys general, and physician lawsuits carrying treble damages.

cards.title: What Sun got wrong

depth.text: An Oxide co-founder argues Sun Microsystems doomed itself by getting bored with the mechanics of running a business.

When an early cloud startup ran on OpenSolaris and tried to buy Sun servers, Sun barely answered the phone and pitched the wrong gear. Dell stepped in within hours, assigning a dedicated rep who arranged financing and delivered leased hardware to the data center in under two weeks.

cards.camps: Two camps: one blames Sun's collapse on horrific customer sales service and proprietary lock-in, while another argues Sun fell because cheap commodity x86 Linux servers destroyed hardware margins while rival internal divisions fought each other.
comments: As someone who was buying hardware in the late 1990s, it is hard to overstate the difference in buying experience between Sun or Digital (DEC) and someone like Dell. Apparently Sun insisted on knowing how many servers Google had, something…

cards.title: If math is more than proof, we need to better celebrate the rest of it

depth.text: Grant Sanderson argues math must reward clear explanations over raw proofs as AI starts generating them

Writing on Terence Tao's blog, Sanderson argued that proofs are only a proxy for human understanding. Because AI can now produce proofs without that understanding, he proposes giving "open exposition problems" the same prestige and academic credit as open research problems.

cards.camps: Two camps: some agree math research has historically over-indexed on proofs at the expense of intuition, while others argue pivoting to explanations will not protect mathematicians because AI can write natural-language explanations too.
comments: I’m reminded of that famous debate between Poincaré and Hilbert at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Paris in 1900. It was then that everyone decided to follow Hilbert’s path, and proof came to be valued more than intuition. I think modern math at school and at applied university kind of lost this intuitive part. I try to teach my students that mathematics is, first and foremost, a…

The math field is confronting something that coders have been dealing with for a few years now, only far more violently. Today's moat for software seems to be that AI can automate tasks but not a full job (yet). But for a large proportion of mathematicians, doing these tasks really was _the_ job. It's the bit they wanted to do, and if they completed a sufficiently difficult set of tasks, they got…

Part of the controversy here is that now the skill advantage that some Field Medalist had is much narrower. The fact that fields medals have an age limit implies that it favors brain power over understanding. And that was the guiding light award of the community. So i find it "funny" (and natural) when they are offended by AI. That is the main "crisis" of mathematics. In my opinion there has…

cards.title: GPT-6 Astra Solves a WWI German Radio Cipher

depth.text: GPT-6 Astra cracked an unsolved 1918 German radio cipher by applying a known key early

The model decrypted an unsolved German ADFGVX radio transmission from November 27, 1918, using the known encryption key word TRUPPENVERSCHIEBUNG. Previous decoders had missed it because that key was officially scheduled for use starting December 9, 1918, but the decrypted text correctly matched historical British naval logs from Sevastopol.

cards.title: English: A vs. An

depth.text: Red Blob Games checked 32,455 words and found only 129 break the simple rule for choosing a or an.

Choosing between 'a' and 'an' depends on whether the spoken word starts with a vowel sound rather than a vowel letter, creating quirks like 'a unicorn' or 'an hour.' Red Blob Games analyzed pronunciation data for procedural text generation to find how often words require special handling.

comments: A funny quirk of English I never noticed until I started learning Spanish: In Spanish, to say for example, "he is a doctor," you would say "él es médico." Which more literally translates to "he is doctor," which feels unintuitive coming from English. Spanish DOES have an equivalent for "a" - "un/una", so the natural thing for an English speaker to say would be "él es UN médico", but I…

What gets me as a non-native speaker far more than "a vs an" is the "a vs the" conundrum. I still don't quite get when something needs to be "indefinite" and I've been speaking English for close to forty years. My native tongue lacks articles altogether and it's soo bloody hard I feel hopeless I'll ever master them fully.

It's avoiding two distinct vowel sounds in succession. Consider other variations of this rule. In French, one would say "l'hôpital" rather than "le hôpital" because the 'h' is an aspirated breath (try saying "a aspirated" rather than "an aspirated") leading to an initial vowel sound. In Irish, the word for father is "athair". To say "her father" it becomes "a hathair"…

As a native speaker of a language without articles, I find the English article system by far the most intuitive and easiest to learn of all the languages I have studied. Most other Indo-European languages have articles that you simply need to memorize, as there is no way to derive them from the word itself. Which I never manage to do.

The most problematic for me as a non-native has been "the" vs "nothing", i.e. when one can/should put the definite article. Pre-LLM I was joking that real AI is whatever can make that decision correctly 100% of times.

cards.title: I think you should almost never use AI to write

depth.text: Erich Grunewald argues you should almost never use AI to write anything substantive

Writing forces you to uncover flaws in your own arguments, which delegating to an AI neatly avoids. On top of that, machine output is often vaguely incorrect in hard-to-spot ways and misleads readers who assume you actually thought through the text.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say fixing AI drafts wastes more time than writing from scratch, while others say endlessly prompting an indefatigable model helps them uncover the exact phrasing they need.
comments: From TFA: "Eric Schwitzgebel writes that . . . There’s a huge cognitive difference between nodding along while reading something and actually productively generating a text. Two reasons: First, once the text is on the page, it’s easy to passively let the approximate word suffice, rather than thinking about word choice in the same effortful, active way we do when generating prose de novo. Second…

Use AI to write things for you to read that you wish someone else had written . ‘Give me a summary of the research on this topic’; ‘Write a report on this data to help me make a decision’. ‘Take this transcript of a meeting and write me the email it could have been’. Don’t use AI to write things that you are producing for someone else to consume.

"AI writing is vague and wrong in hard-to-notice ways" This one felt to me, at work I lost a lot of time re-reading and correcting AI prose that was launched to "summarize" a collective white paper, and where subtlety and nuance disappeared in ways that harmed the initial ideas/arguments I was writing about, but in sneaky ways.

Instead of asking AI to write something substansive for you, ask it to critique your writing. Then use your own judgement as to which bits of advice to follow and which to ignore. The LLM will always give you a full rewrite — don't use it. It always does too much, and persuading it to tone it down is a constant battle.

I can't help but think that some of the arguments here apply equally well to writing _code_ as they to to other substantive writings. Writing code is thinking, AI code is often vague and wrong in hard-to-notice ways, and the (human) reader of code is the one that pays the cost for this later. The cost/benefit analysis may still work out differently for code though...

cards.title: MCP was always a bad idea?

depth.text: a developer declared MCP obsolete because modern models can just use CLIs and call APIs directly

Maharshi Patel argued that MCP was designed for less capable models and has become obsolete now that agents can write scripts and execute terminal commands. He urged teams to delete their MCP servers and standardize direct HTTP API calls instead of managing tool context bloat.

cards.camps: Two camps: one side agrees that terminal-enabled agents can replace MCP servers with simple CLI and API scripts, while the other insists MCP remains crucial for audit logging, credential safety, and agents that lack command line access.
comments: This article entirely misses the value that MCP brings today. Sure, there's almost no reason to use MCPs if you are running a full-blown terminal agent (Claude Code, Codex, Meta Muse, OpenClaw etc) with unfettered internet access - just let it call APIs directly. If you want to operate something that's less YOLO than that, you'll find yourself wanting: 1. Control over exactly which external…

MCPs are winning because within the ChatGPT and Claude apps, there are Plugin stores. These plugins are one-click installation MCP servers, with support for authentication. This is what business users are using.

MCP is like anything else - it has its uses. Use it where it makes sense. Where it doesn't, don't. For my part, I probably rarely want my Agent to waste time writing its own adapter for a particular API that needs to be called, when I can just point it at an existing MCP server. cards.title: The Effect of CRTs on Pixel Art (2024)

depth.text: a retro developer argued that CRTs never erased pixels, and that modern blocky art comes from sloppy technique

The author argues that classic pixel art looked smooth because artists painstakingly used dithering and anti-aliasing within tight constraints, not because cathode ray tubes inherently hid pixels. Late-stage computer CRTs and RGB monitors displayed sharp, visible pixels, while extreme blur came down to low-end consumer televisions and composite signals. Modern pixel art often skips these traditional techniques entirely, making games look chunkier than originals ever did.

cards.camps: Two camps: some consider modern blocky pixel art its own valid art form tailored for high-resolution displays, while retro purists insist classic games only look right with authentic CRT curves, scanlines, and hardware quirks.
comments: I like to think of modern pixel art as its own aesthetic and art form. It's designed to be viewed on high DPI LED screens, and that's fine. I don't think it should be judged by how it looks on a CRT. There's an undeniable charm to the older era of pixel art, and surely part of that is nostalgia, but I also think a lot of it comes from the fact that the economics and the hardware were a lot…

> I don't know if the CRT version is taken from an actual CRT, but I doubt it - I actually think it looks too fuzzy. I may be wrong - it could be an effect of a close-up photo scaled up - but it's more likely a CRT approximation generated by a software filter on a modern machine. On both the NES and SNES, the pixels were so large that you could clearly see them even when using an RF adaptor. Each…

It's not that CRTs were "forgiving", it's that designers leaned into what they'd do to pixels. A classic example is the tanks in Atari 2600 Combat - they look ridiculous on a hi-res screen. But it's…

cards.title: Why do we need human mathematicians anymore?

depth.text: Po-Shen Loh argued that AI will create so many oversight jobs that progress will be forced to slow down

Loh argues that AI creates an explosion of untrusted decisions and vulnerable control points that demand skilled human oversight. To steer these systems effectively, people must remain active practitioners at the research frontier rather than passive watchers. Because of this dynamic, AI labs will eventually have to slow their pace or face disasters caused by exhausting human control.

cards.title: Singapore’s National Library Board offers micropayments to build reading habits

depth.text: Singapore's National Library Board is paying people tiny cash rewards to put down their phones and read books.

Under the ReadSG pilot on the CrowdTaskSG platform, logging 15 minutes of reading earns 20 virtual coins. Only one session counts daily, so earning a single Singapore dollar takes fifty consecutive days. The library board described the tiny payout as a behavioral nudge rather than an income stream.

cards.title: What Zig felt like, coming from Rust

depth.text: A veteran Rust developer ported a library to Zig and ran into manual allocators and missing tooling.

After seven years writing Rust, the author ported their JSONPath parser to Zig, which replaced functional patterns with imperative mutation. The transition required passing allocators everywhere and manually coordinating cleanup calls, reintroducing leaks and double-free bugs eliminated by Rust's compiler.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters argue that skipping automatic destructors is a dead end that dooms projects to memory leaks and crashes, while others contend that Zig provides a cleaner, practical alternative to C that avoids Rust's steep cognitive overhead.

cards.title: US Revokes Limits on Power Plants' Climate Pollution

depth.text: The EPA repealed carbon emissions limits on power plants, arguing that greenhouse gases do not impact climate change.

The rollback guts 2024 standards that required coal plants and new gas plants to capture 90 percent of emissions or close by 2039. The agency said the move saves businesses $370 million in compliance costs, after deciding to stop factoring public health impacts into its economic estimates.

cards.camps: Two camps: most say gutting the rules harms public health and clings to uncompetitive fuels, while a few argue the change is minor or question defining carbon dioxide as pollution.
